title: the Sri Sukta
hook: a fruit with a shell you need a hammer for, and a tree the hymn says was born from the goddess's discipline

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta turned and spoke to her directly: I take refuge, I choose you. Whom did you speak to, instead of about? Today, a tree. Day one thousand ninety-six.

The bilva fruit does not look generous. It's round and greenish-gold, and its shell is so hard that people crack it against a stone step or with the back of a cleaver. You have to work to get in. Inside is a sticky, fragrant pulp that some families stir into a cool summer drink. A goddess of abundance might be expected to have a softer fruit. A mango, maybe. But when the Sri Sukta names her tree, it names this one, the bilva. And it says where the tree came from.
screen: `A SHELL YOU NEED A HAMMER FOR.` → `FRAGRANT PULP INSIDE.` → `HER TREE IS THE BILVA.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in paraphrase. O you who are the color of the sun, from your tapas the lord of the forest was born: your tree, the bilva. May its fruits, by tapas, drive away the misfortunes within and without. Start with the word tapas. It means heat, and then the heat of discipline: effort, austerity, the steady inner fire of someone who keeps at a hard practice. In the old stories, it's the fire sages keep burning in the forest, through steady practice. And here's the surprise. The hymn gives tapas to Sri. The goddess of fortune, gold and ease is the one whose discipline makes the tree grow. In this line, abundance isn't the opposite of effort. It comes out of it. Then the tree itself. Lord of the forest is an old way of saying a great tree. And its fruits have a job: to push away misfortune. Notice that the fruit does it by tapas too. The same heat that grew the tree works through what it bears. Now the last phrase, misfortunes within and without. The outer ones are easy to list: a failed harvest, an empty purse, a roof that leaks. The inner ones are harder to name. Some readers hear confusion there, illusion, the habits of mind that block a person from within. Others hear the plain sense, trouble inside the house as well as outside it. Either way, the hymn won't let fortune be only something that happens out there. And it chose a fruit you can't open without effort. Some readers find that fitting: the good thing is inside, and getting to it takes a little heat.
screen: `THE COLOR OF THE SUN.` · `TAPAS, THE HEAT OF DISCIPLINE.` · `HER TREE, THE BILVA.` · `MISFORTUNE WITHIN AND WITHOUT.` · then, large: `ABUNDANCE GROWN FROM EFFORT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a little heat. Sit up, settle, and let the breath slow. Then choose to stay still, really still, for the whole sit, even when something itches or the mind wants to wander off. That's tapas at its smallest: staying with a thing a little longer than is comfortable. Notice the small warmth of effort, and don't make it a strain. If the mind wanders, bring it back, again and again; the bringing back is the practice. If you pray, you can offer the effort to the goddess, or to God, in your own words. If you don't, let the stillness be its own offering. The bell holds the time.
The Sri Sukta. A hymn that says the bilva tree was born from the goddess's own tapas, and asks its fruit to drive away misfortune within and without.
Your line: the Sri Sukta. Today, pick one hard-shelled task you've been avoiding, and give it ten honest minutes. Day one thousand ninety-six.

howItsDone: The bilva tree is treated as sacred in Hindu worship, where its leaves are offered, and this verse is recited as part of the Sri Sukta in Lakshmi worship.

fork.setup: you're writing a hymn to the goddess of abundance and need to say where her sacred tree came from. what do you say?
options: it simply appeared, effortless, like all her gifts.
it was born from her tapas, her discipline.
a king planted it for her.
fork.reveal: the Sri Sukta says the bilva was born from her tapas: in this line, abundance grows out of effort.

original.note: Sanskrit: bilvaḥ, the bilva tree (bael), which the Sri Sukta calls hers, born from her tapas.

trapdoor: what you thought: a goddess of abundance hands out ease.
what it means: the hymn says her own discipline grew her tree, and its fruit pushes away misfortune inside and out.
what a scholar hears: tapaso 'dhijāto vanaspatis tava vṛkṣo 'tha bilvaḥ: tapas, the creative heat of Vedic thought, given to Sri herself.

sources.ref: Sri Sukta, verse 6 (Rig Veda khila, as commonly recited)

notes: Verse 6 paraphrased: ādityavarṇe tapaso 'dhijāto vanaspatis tava vṛkṣo 'tha bilvaḥ / tasya phalāni tapasā nudantu māyāntarāyāś ca bāhyā alakṣmīḥ. māyāntarāyāḥ is read variously ('illusions and inner obstacles', 'misfortunes within'); the script gives two readings without ranking. Confirm.
'In the old stories, it's the fire sages keep burning in the forest' refers to tapas in earlier Hindu path lessons; confirm it was taught.
Bilva (Aegle marmelos, bael): hard shell and pulp used in a summer drink are everyday descriptions; confirm. howItsDone says bilva leaves are offered in worship (common in Shiva worship).
'Some readers find that fitting' (the hard shell as image of effort) is an interpretive image; confirm or cut.
Editor pass: the teach's line on tapas and forest sages was reworded (it repeated 'keeping at' twice and read as a flat claim about all old stories); the garbled quote in the note above was repaired.
